title: The first haircut
hookLine: at three, in many Hasidic and some Sephardi families

cards: A little boy sits on his father's lap, curls down past his shoulders. He has never had a haircut.
The living room is full of relatives and neighbors, and a pair of scissors is going around the room like a microphone at a wedding.
One by one, each guest snips a single lock: an uncle, a grandmother, the rabbi, a cousin barely taller than the boy. Somebody's handing out candy.
By the end he looks like a different child, and at the sides of his head, two locks have been left long, on purpose.

teach.h: THREE YEARS, LIKE A YOUNG TREE.
teach.b: Upsherin. A Yiddish name for a child's first haircut, held at three in many Hasidic families and, in their own versions, in some Sephardi families too. First, the tree.
Leviticus says that when Israel plants a fruit tree, its fruit is not to be eaten for three years. In the fourth year it is holy, and after that it is food.
And the Deuteronomy verse about fruit trees in a siege is read by some as comparing a person to a tree of the field.
Some families draw the line between the two: a child, like a young tree, is left untouched for three years, and then the first harvest. It's a custom, not a written law. Second, the side locks.

Leviticus also says not to round off the corners of the head. So at the first haircut, the hair at the temples is left long. These are the peyot, the side locks, and for the boy they start on this day.
In some families, an upsherin is also the day a boy first wears a kippah and the fringed garment called tzitzit, and some bring him to start learning his letters that week.
The haircut is the outward sign; the inner change is that the child now begins to be taught.
Fourth, the whole room. The custom doesn't give the scissors to a barber alone. Each guest takes a turn, and everyone who snips a curl has a hand in raising this child.

how: In many Hasidic families, and in some Sephardi families with their own versions, a boy's hair is left uncut until he turns three; at the upsherin, guests each cut a lock, the side locks are left, and he often begins wearing a kippah and tzitzit.

games.q: you're a guest at an upsherin, and the scissors reach you. what does custom ask?
o: snip one lock and pass the scissors on.
games.why: each guest snips a single lock, so everyone has a hand in raising the child.

practice: Think of something that has been growing quietly in your life, a child, a friendship, a skill, a garden, a recovery, something you've been patient with, and ask whether it has reached a point worth marking.
Picture the people who'd have a hand in it, each taking a turn. Then choose one small way to mark it, a meal, a message, a few words said out loud, and if you pray, give thanks for what has grown.

wordCard.voice: Upsherin. The first haircut at three: the young tree, the side locks left long, and a turn with the scissors for everyone. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: three years. First the waiting, then a whole room leans in. One more step on the hill.
